description: Time value of money, option pricing, portfolio optimization and performance measurement, plus time-series model specification, estimation, diagnostic testing, forecasting and simulation.

tools.name: pvfix
tools.description: Compute the present value of a series of equal periodic cash flows plus an optional lump sum at the end. The due flag switches between ordinary annuities (payment at period end) and annuities due (payment at period start). It is the basic discounting calculation for loans, leases and bond-like instruments.
tools.usage:
PresentVal = pvfix(Rate, NumPeriods, Payment)
PresentVal = pvfix(Rate, NumPeriods, Payment, ExtraPayment, Due)

parameters.name: Rate
parameters.description: Periodic interest rate as a decimal, e.g. 0.05/12 for a monthly rate.

parameters.name: NumPeriods
parameters.description: Number of periods.

parameters.name: Payment
parameters.description: Equal periodic cash flow.

parameters.name: ExtraPayment
parameters.description: Additional lump sum received at the end (default 0).

parameters.name: Due
parameters.description: 0 for end-of-period payments (default), 1 for beginning-of-period.

tools.notes: pvvar handles irregular cash flows; fvfix computes the corresponding future value.

tools.name: fvfix
tools.description: Compute the future value of a series of equal periodic payments compounded at a fixed rate, plus an optional present lump sum. It answers how much a regular savings plan will be worth at the end of its term. The due flag handles payments made at the start of each period.
tools.usage:
FutureVal = fvfix(Rate, NumPeriods, Payment)
FutureVal = fvfix(Rate, NumPeriods, Payment, PresentVal, Due)

parameters.name: Rate
parameters.description: Periodic interest rate as a decimal.

parameters.name: NumPeriods
parameters.description: Number of compounding periods.

parameters.name: Payment
parameters.description: Equal periodic contribution.

parameters.name: PresentVal
parameters.description: Initial lump sum (default 0).

parameters.name: Due
parameters.description: 0 (end of period, default) or 1 (beginning).

tools.name: irr
tools.description: Compute the internal rate of return of a cash flow series, that is the discount rate at which the net present value is zero. Sign changes in the cash flows can produce multiple real roots, so the second output lists all of them. Use it to compare projects on a rate-of-return basis.
tools.usage:
Return = irr(CashFlow)
[Return, AllRates] = irr(CashFlow)

parameters.name: CashFlow
parameters.description: Vector or matrix of cash flows, with the initial (usually negative) investment first; each column is a separate series.

tools.notes: IRR is unreliable when cash flows change sign more than once; compare NPV at a fixed discount rate instead.

tools.name: pvvar
tools.description: Compute the present value of a series of irregular, varying cash flows at a given discount rate, optionally with explicit dates for non-uniform spacing. Unlike pvfix it makes no assumption that the payments are equal. It is the general-purpose NPV calculation for project appraisal.
tools.usage:
PresentVal = pvvar(CashFlow, Rate)
PresentVal = pvvar(CashFlow, Rate, CFDates)

parameters.name: CashFlow
parameters.description: Vector of cash flows, first element at time zero.

parameters.name: Rate
parameters.description: Periodic (or annual, when dates are given) discount rate.

parameters.name: CFDates
parameters.description: Serial date numbers or datetimes for irregularly spaced flows.

tools.name: blsprice
tools.description: Compute European call and put option prices with the Black-Scholes-Merton formula, including a continuous dividend yield. It returns both the call and the put value, which satisfy put-call parity. It is the reference pricing model against which more complex models are calibrated.
tools.usage:
[Call, Put] = blsprice(Price, Strike, Rate, Time, Volatility)
[Call, Put] = blsprice(Price, Strike, Rate, Time, Volatility, Yield)

parameters.name: Price
parameters.description: Current price of the underlying asset.

parameters.name: Strike
parameters.description: Exercise price.

parameters.name: Rate
parameters.description: Annualized continuously compounded risk-free rate.

parameters.name: Time
parameters.description: Time to expiry in years.

parameters.name: Volatility
parameters.description: Annualized volatility as a decimal.

parameters.name: Yield
parameters.description: Continuous dividend yield (default 0).

tools.notes: blsdelta, blsgamma, blsvega, blstheta and blsrho give the Greeks with the same argument list.

tools.name: blsimpv
tools.description: Solve for the implied volatility that makes the Black-Scholes price equal an observed market option price. Implied volatility is the market's forward-looking estimate of risk and is the standard quoting convention for options. It returns NaN when no volatility can reproduce the given price.
tools.usage:
Volatility = blsimpv(Price, Strike, Rate, Time, Value)
Volatility = blsimpv(___, Limit, Yield, Tolerance, Class)
Volatility = blsimpv(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Value
parameters.description: Observed market price of the option.

parameters.name: Limit
parameters.description: Upper bound of the volatility search (default 10).

parameters.name: Yield
parameters.description: Continuous dividend yield.

parameters.name: Class
parameters.description: true or {'call'} for calls, false or {'put'} for puts.

parameters.name: 'Method'
parameters.description: 'search' (default) or 'jackel2016' for a fast analytic approximation.

tools.name: Portfolio
tools.description: Build a mean-variance portfolio optimization problem, holding the asset return moments, the budget and bound constraints, and any turnover, group or tracking-error limits. Its methods estimate the efficient frontier, find the maximum Sharpe ratio portfolio and compute risk and return for any weights. It is the core object of modern portfolio theory in MATLAB.
tools.usage:
p = Portfolio
p = Portfolio(Name, Value)
p = setAssetMoments(p, mean, covariance)
p = estimateAssetMoments(p, returns)
p = setDefaultConstraints(p)
w = estimateFrontier(p, n)

parameters.name: 'AssetMean' / 'AssetCovar'
parameters.description: Expected returns vector and covariance matrix.

parameters.name: 'NumAssets'
parameters.description: Number of assets in the universe.

parameters.name: 'LowerBound' / 'UpperBound'
parameters.description: Per-asset weight bounds.

parameters.name: 'RiskFreeRate'
parameters.description: Risk-free rate used for Sharpe ratio calculations.

parameters.name: 'Budget'
parameters.description: Total weight constraint, usually 1 for a fully invested portfolio.

parameters.name: 'Turnover' / 'TrackingError'
parameters.description: Optional trading and benchmark-deviation constraints.

tools.notes: PortfolioCVaR and PortfolioMAD offer conditional-value-at-risk and mean-absolute-deviation alternatives.

tools.name: estimateFrontier
tools.description: Compute portfolio weights along the efficient frontier, returning the optimal allocation at a number of equally spaced points between the minimum-risk and maximum-return portfolios. Every returned portfolio satisfies all the constraints set on the Portfolio object. Its outputs feed estimatePortMoments and plotFrontier.
tools.usage:
pwgt = estimateFrontier(obj)
pwgt = estimateFrontier(obj, NumPorts)
[pwgt, pbuy, psell] = estimateFrontier(___)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: A Portfolio, PortfolioCVaR or PortfolioMAD object with moments and constraints set.

parameters.name: NumPorts
parameters.description: Number of frontier points to compute (default 10).

parameters.name: pbuy, psell
parameters.description: Purchases and sales relative to the initial portfolio, when one is set.

tools.name: estimateMaxSharpeRatio
tools.description: Find the portfolio on the efficient frontier that maximizes the Sharpe ratio, that is excess return per unit of risk. This is the tangency portfolio, the optimal risky portfolio to combine with a risk-free asset. It respects every constraint configured on the Portfolio object.
tools.usage:
pwgt = estimateMaxSharpeRatio(obj)
[pwgt, pbuy, psell] = estimateMaxSharpeRatio(obj)
pwgt = estimateMaxSharpeRatio(obj, 'Method', method)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: A Portfolio object with a RiskFreeRate set.

parameters.name: 'Method'
parameters.description: 'iterative' (default) or 'direct'.

parameters.name: 'TolX'
parameters.description: Termination tolerance for the iterative method.

tools.name: tick2ret
tools.description: Convert a price series into periodic returns, either simple (arithmetic) or continuous (logarithmic). Return series are stationary and additive in log form, which is what almost every financial model requires as input. ret2tick performs the inverse reconstruction.
tools.usage:
returns = tick2ret(data)
[returns, intervals] = tick2ret(data, Name, Value)

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Price matrix, table or timetable; each column is an asset.

parameters.name: 'Method'
parameters.description: 'simple' (default) or 'continuous' for log returns.

parameters.name: 'DataFormat'
parameters.description: Layout hint when input rows are variables rather than observations.

tools.name: maxdrawdown
tools.description: Compute the maximum peak-to-trough decline of a price or equity series, along with the indices where the peak and trough occur. Maximum drawdown is the standard measure of downside risk for a trading strategy, because it captures the worst loss an investor would actually have lived through. Arithmetic, geometric and return-series modes are supported.
tools.usage:
MaxDD = maxdrawdown(Data)
[MaxDD, MaxDDIndex] = maxdrawdown(Data)
[MaxDD, MaxDDIndex] = maxdrawdown(Data, Format)

parameters.name: Data
parameters.description: Series of total equity values or prices, one column per series.

parameters.name: Format
parameters.description: 'return' (default, relative drawdown), 'arithmetic' or 'geometric'.

tools.name: sharpe
tools.description: Compute the Sharpe ratio of one or more return series: mean excess return divided by its standard deviation. It is the most widely used risk-adjusted performance measure, though it penalizes upside volatility as much as downside. Annualize it by multiplying by the square root of the number of periods per year.
tools.usage:
ratio = sharpe(Asset)
ratio = sharpe(Asset, Cash)

parameters.name: Asset
parameters.description: Matrix of asset returns, one column per series.

parameters.name: Cash
parameters.description: Risk-free return per period, scalar or a series (default 0).

tools.notes: sortino uses downside deviation instead, and inforatio measures performance against a benchmark.

tools.name: movavg
tools.description: Compute moving averages of a price series using simple, exponential, triangular, weighted or modified weighting. Crossovers between a fast and a slow average form the basis of many trend-following trading rules. It accepts matrices, tables and timetables.
tools.usage:
ma = movavg(Data, type, windowSize)
[ma, secondMA] = movavg(Data, type, [lead lag])
ma = movavg(Data, type, windowSize, initialPoints)

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: 'simple', 'square-root', 'linear', 'exponential', 'triangular', 'modified', 'custom'.

parameters.name: windowSize
parameters.description: Averaging window length, or [lead lag] for two averages at once.

parameters.name: initialPoints
parameters.description: 'shrink' (default) or 'fill' to handle the start of the series.

tools.name: arima
tools.description: Specify an ARIMA(p,D,q) model, optionally with seasonal terms, a regression component and a conditional-variance model such as GARCH. Unknown parameters are left as NaN and filled in by estimate. The resulting model object supports forecasting, simulation and residual inference.
tools.usage:
Mdl = arima(p, D, q)
Mdl = arima(Name, Value)
EstMdl = estimate(Mdl, y)
[yF, yMSE] = forecast(EstMdl, numPeriods, 'Y0', y)
Y = simulate(EstMdl, numObs)

parameters.name: p, D, q
parameters.description: Autoregressive order, degree of differencing, and moving-average order.

parameters.name: 'Constant'
parameters.description: Model constant; set to 0 to exclude it.

parameters.name: 'Seasonality' / 'SAR' / 'SMA'
parameters.description: Seasonal differencing period and seasonal lag polynomials.

parameters.name: 'Distribution'
parameters.description: 'Gaussian' (default) or 't' for heavy-tailed innovations.

parameters.name: 'Variance'
parameters.description: A scalar, or a garch/egarch/gjr model for conditional heteroscedasticity.

tools.name: garch
tools.description: Specify a GARCH(P,Q) conditional variance model, which captures the volatility clustering seen in financial returns. Leave the parameters as NaN for estimate to fit them by maximum likelihood. Use it alone on a return series or as the Variance property of an arima model.
tools.usage:
Mdl = garch(P, Q)
Mdl = garch(Name, Value)
EstMdl = estimate(Mdl, y)
v = infer(EstMdl, y)
[V, Y] = simulate(EstMdl, numObs)
vF = forecast(EstMdl, numPeriods, 'Y0', y)

parameters.name: P
parameters.description: Number of lagged conditional variance terms.

parameters.name: Q
parameters.description: Number of lagged squared innovation (ARCH) terms.

parameters.name: 'Offset'
parameters.description: Mean of the innovation process; set to NaN to estimate it.

parameters.name: 'Distribution'
parameters.description: 'Gaussian' (default) or 't' for fat-tailed returns.

parameters.name: 'Constant' / 'GARCH' / 'ARCH'
parameters.description: Parameter values, NaN where unknown.

tools.notes: egarch and gjr add asymmetry so that negative returns raise volatility more than positive ones.

tools.name: estimate
tools.description: Fit the unknown parameters of an econometric model to data by maximum likelihood, returning a fully specified model plus standard errors and a fit summary. It works for arima, garch, varm, ssm, regARIMA and the other model classes with the same basic signature. Presample data can be supplied so that no observations are lost to initialization.
tools.usage:
EstMdl = estimate(Mdl, y)
[EstMdl, EstParamCov, logL, info] = estimate(Mdl, y, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Mdl
parameters.description: A model object with NaN placeholders for the parameters to estimate.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Observed response series.

parameters.name: 'Y0' / 'E0' / 'V0'
parameters.description: Presample responses, innovations and variances.

parameters.name: 'X'
parameters.description: Predictor data for regression components.

parameters.name: 'Display'
parameters.description: 'params' (default), 'full', 'off', 'diagnostics', 'iter'.

parameters.name: 'Options'
parameters.description: optimoptions for fmincon controlling the likelihood maximization.

tools.name: forecast
tools.description: Generate minimum-mean-square-error forecasts from a fitted model, together with the forecast error variances needed for confidence intervals. Supplying presample data through 'Y0' conditions the forecast on the actual history rather than on the unconditional mean. It works across arima, garch, varm and ssm models.
tools.usage:
[Y, YMSE] = forecast(Mdl, numPeriods)
[Y, YMSE] = forecast(Mdl, numPeriods, 'Y0', Y0)
[Y, YMSE, V] = forecast(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: numPeriods
parameters.description: Forecast horizon.

parameters.name: 'Y0'
parameters.description: Presample response data on which to condition.

parameters.name: 'E0' / 'V0'
parameters.description: Presample innovations and conditional variances.

parameters.name: 'X' / 'XF'
parameters.description: In-sample and future predictor data for regression models.

tools.name: simulate
tools.description: Generate random sample paths from a fitted or fully specified econometric model. Monte Carlo paths are how you build forecast distributions, value-at-risk estimates and bootstrap confidence bands for statistics with no closed form. Set rng beforehand for reproducible results.
tools.usage:
Y = simulate(Mdl, numObs)
Y = simulate(Mdl, numObs, 'NumPaths', n)
[Y, E, V] = simulate(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: numObs
parameters.description: Length of each simulated path.

parameters.name: 'NumPaths'
parameters.description: Number of independent paths (default 1).

parameters.name: 'Y0' / 'E0' / 'V0'
parameters.description: Presample data to condition the simulation on.

parameters.name: 'X'
parameters.description: Predictor data for regression components.

tools.name: infer
tools.description: Infer the unobserved innovations and conditional variances of a fitted model from the observed data. The inferred residuals are what you test for remaining autocorrelation and ARCH effects during model validation. It also returns the loglikelihood contribution of each observation.
tools.usage:
E = infer(Mdl, Y)
[E, V, logL] = infer(Mdl, Y)
[___] = infer(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: Mdl
parameters.description: A fully specified (estimated) model object.

parameters.name: Y
parameters.description: Observed response data.

parameters.name: 'Y0' / 'E0' / 'V0'
parameters.description: Presample data.

parameters.name: 'X'
parameters.description: Predictor data for regression components.

tools.name: adftest
tools.description: Augmented Dickey-Fuller test for a unit root in a univariate time series, whose null hypothesis is that the series is non-stationary. Rejecting the null supports stationarity, which most time-series models require. The model option and lag length materially affect the result, so test several specifications.
tools.usage:
h = adftest(y)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = adftest(y, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Model'
parameters.description: 'AR' (default, no drift), 'ARD' (with drift), 'TS' (with drift and trend).

parameters.name: 'Lags'
parameters.description: Number of lagged difference terms; scalar or vector to test several.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level (default 0.05).

parameters.name: 'Test'
parameters.description: 't1' (default), 't2' or 'F' statistic variant.

tools.notes: The ADF test has low power; confirm with kpsstest, which reverses the null hypothesis.

tools.name: kpsstest
tools.description: KPSS test for stationarity, whose null hypothesis is that the series is trend- or level-stationary, the reverse of the ADF test. Running both tests together gives a much more reliable conclusion than either alone. Failing to reject KPSS while rejecting ADF is strong evidence of stationarity.
tools.usage:
h = kpsstest(y)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = kpsstest(y, Name, Value)

parameters.name: 'Lags'
parameters.description: Number of autocovariance lags in the Newey-West variance estimator.

parameters.name: 'Trend'
parameters.description: Logical; true (default) tests trend stationarity, false tests level stationarity.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level.

tools.notes: p-values are reported as the table bounds 0.01 and 0.10 when the statistic falls outside the tabulated range.

tools.name: lbqtest
tools.description: Ljung-Box Q-test for residual autocorrelation up to a specified lag, whose null hypothesis is that the series has no serial correlation. Applied to model residuals it tests whether the model has captured all the linear dependence. Applied to squared residuals it tests for remaining ARCH effects.
tools.usage:
h = lbqtest(res)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = lbqtest(res, Name, Value)

parameters.name: res
parameters.description: Residual series to test.

parameters.name: 'Lags'
parameters.description: Number of lags to include in the Q statistic.

parameters.name: 'DOF'
parameters.description: Degrees of freedom, normally Lags minus the number of estimated model parameters.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level.

tools.name: archtest
tools.description: Engle's ARCH test for conditional heteroscedasticity, whose null hypothesis is that there are no ARCH effects in the residuals. Rejecting it means volatility clusters and a GARCH-family variance model is warranted. Run it on the residuals of a fitted mean model, not on the raw series.
tools.usage:
h = archtest(res)
[h, pValue, stat, cValue] = archtest(res, Name, Value)

parameters.name: res
parameters.description: Residual series from a fitted conditional mean model.

parameters.name: 'Lags'
parameters.description: Number of lagged squared residuals in the test regression.

parameters.name: 'Alpha'
parameters.description: Significance level.

tools.name: varm
tools.description: Specify a vector autoregression model for several interdependent time series, where each variable depends on lagged values of all of them. It supports exogenous regressors, deterministic trends and Gaussian or t innovations. Use it for macroeconomic modelling, impulse response analysis and Granger causality testing.
tools.usage:
Mdl = varm(numSeries, numLags)
Mdl = varm(Name, Value)
EstMdl = estimate(Mdl, Y)
[Y, YMSE] = forecast(EstMdl, numPeriods, Y0)
irf(EstMdl)

parameters.name: numSeries
parameters.description: Number of response variables.

parameters.name: numLags
parameters.description: Autoregressive order.

parameters.name: 'Constant' / 'Trend'
parameters.description: Deterministic terms; NaN marks them for estimation.

parameters.name: 'Beta'
parameters.description: Coefficients on exogenous predictors.

parameters.name: 'Covariance'
parameters.description: Innovation covariance matrix.

parameters.name: 'SeriesNames'
parameters.description: Names used in displays and plots.

tools.notes: vecm handles cointegrated systems; use jcitest first to check for cointegration.

tools.name: autocorr
tools.description: Compute and plot the sample autocorrelation function with approximate confidence bounds. The decay pattern of the ACF identifies the moving-average order of an ARIMA model and reveals seasonality and non-stationarity. Called with no output arguments it produces the standard stem plot.
tools.usage:
autocorr(y)
acf = autocorr(y, Name, Value)
[acf, lags, bounds] = autocorr(y)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Time series, preferably already made stationary.

parameters.name: 'NumLags'
parameters.description: Number of lags to compute (default min(20, N-1)).

parameters.name: 'NumMA'
parameters.description: Assumed MA order used when computing the confidence bounds.

parameters.name: 'NumSTD'
parameters.description: Number of standard deviations for the bounds (default 2).

tools.name: parcorr
tools.description: Compute and plot the sample partial autocorrelation function, which measures the correlation at each lag after removing the effect of the intervening lags. A sharp cut-off after lag p indicates an AR(p) process, complementing the ACF's identification of MA order. Confidence bounds are shown automatically in the plot.
tools.usage:
parcorr(y)
pacf = parcorr(y, Name, Value)
[pacf, lags, bounds] = parcorr(y)

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Time series to analyse.

parameters.name: 'NumLags'
parameters.description: Number of lags to compute.

parameters.name: 'NumAR'
parameters.description: Assumed AR order for the confidence bounds.

parameters.name: 'Method'
parameters.description: 'ols' (default) or 'yule-walker'.
